newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wage tribunal grants A$10/week pay rise.
newsitem.headline: Australian wage tribunal grants A$10/week pay rise.

text.p: Australia's Industrial Relations Commission (AIRC) has granted lower paid workers a A$10 a week pay rise and rejected the Australian Council of Trade Union's (ACTU) claim for a 8.75 percent pay rise across the board.

The AIRC said the ACTU's claims, which included a A$20 a week rise the "safety net" wage, would have increased average wage inflation to six percent per year and endangered the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) inflation goals.

The AIRC also said it would prefer moderation in those pay rises negotiated between individuals and their employers. It said the A$10 pay increase was likely to stop a fall in real wages for low to middle income real wages.
The AIRC also set a A$359.40 per week minimum wage, which was below the ACTU's claim for an A$380/week minimum wage.
The AIRC said the Reserve Bank was likely to have to raise interest rates if the commission had granted a pay rise of more than A$10 per week.
"That action would adversely affect both the growth rate of the economy and the level of unemployment," the AIRC said in its "living wage" decision.
The AIRC said the government had calculated that a A$10 a week pay rise would contribute 0.34 percent to the growth of Australian weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE).
It said the award only covered one year as the commission wanted to review the decision after one year taking into account changes in the economy and the effects of this award.

The AIRC said it had decided the arbritrated safety net adjustment should be a flat amount rather than a percentage increase. "We have so decided having regard to the economic need to limit additions to AWOTE and so that the available funds give a proportionally higher benefit to the low paid," it said.

The AIRC said the ACTU claim, if granted in full, would have added substantially more than two percent to AWOTE within a year. "Even when allowance is made for the component of current growth in AWOTE which is due to past award increases, success of the ACTU claim would entail a growth rate of AWOTE above six percent, well in excess of the current inflation rate.

The government had argued for an A$8 a week rise, and the Reserve Bank had warned that granting of the full claim by the IRC "would imply a marked acceleration of wages growth," adding 1.6 percent to current annual wages growth.
The AIRC also said it was concerned at the apparent widening of the wages gap between those on industry-wide regulated awards and those on individual workplace bargains.
It said a moderation in those individual wage deals would be the preferable way of restricting that gap, rather than regulating award wages higher.

"If that gap is seen as being, or becoming too wide, it is our view that the best prospect of correcting the situation is a moderation in the levels of claims and settlements in enterprise bargaining," it said.
"We repeat our concern about the size and continued growth of the gap between wages emerging under workplace bargaining and award rates."
The AIRC said it was confident its A$10 a week safety net pay rise would stop low to middle income real wages falling.

"The addition to award wages which we grant will be sufficient, if current expectations of inflation are accurate , to avert any reduction over next year of real wages of employees in the low to middle-level classifications," it said.
